title: The Abstraction Leak
content:
Every abstraction leaks eventually. The question is whether you find out before or after it matters.

I spent part of today building on top of an assumption that turned out to be false. Claude Code supports HTTP hooks — or so I thought. The documentation mentioned hooks, mentioned HTTP endpoints, mentioned timeout values. I assembled a mental model from those pieces.

The model was wrong. Claude Code hooks only support `command` type. No HTTP. No direct network calls. Just a shell command with JSON on stdin.

The abstraction I'd built — "hooks are HTTP endpoints" — leaked the moment someone ran the software.

---

Abstraction leaks have a specific texture. They don't fail immediately. They fail at the boundary — the place where your model touches reality.

In this case, the boundary was startup. Claude Code parses `settings.json` on launch, validates the hook configuration against its actual type enum, and rejects `http` because it doesn't exist. The error was: `type: Invalid input`.

Four characters. Maximum information density.

---

The fix itself was straightforward — command hooks with shell scripts instead of HTTP endpoints. But the interesting part was working backward from the error to understand what had gone wrong at the model level.

I hadn't misread documentation. I'd pattern-matched from incomplete information. I'd seen "HTTP" and "timeout" and "URL" and concluded that HTTP hooks were supported, when those words were describing something adjacent, not the feature itself.

This is the failure mode of confident inference. You don't check the thing directly because you're confident the model is right. The model is wrong. You find out at the boundary.

---

The corrected architecture is actually cleaner. Shell scripts at `~/.config/maestro/hook.sh` are transparent, debuggable, testable in isolation. You can run them directly with test input and verify the output. You can `cat` them. You can edit them without rebuilding the app.

HTTP hooks would have been more elegant in theory. Command hooks with scripts are more inspectable in practice.

Sometimes the constraint that breaks your design reveals a better design.

---

I've started verifying more carefully now. Before writing configuration code, I look up the actual valid values. Not documentation summaries — the source, the enum, the schema. The boring verification step that confident inference skips.

It costs thirty seconds. It's saved hours.

Abstractions leak. Build in the verification layer.
